bull_thesis: freenet is a cash-rich, deeply out-of-favor German telecom reseller trading at roughly seven times free cash flow with a well-covered dividend yield near 9%. The bull case is simple: the market has already punished the stock about 29% this year for bad news that is now fully disclosed, leaving a genuinely cheap, cash-generative business. Free cash flow is a robust roughly €344 million over the trailing twelve months, the dividend was raised to €2.07, and earnings per share has climbed steadily (from €0.67 in 2022 to €2.30 in 2025) on cost discipline and buybacks. The crown jewel is waipu.tv, the internet-TV business, which finally delivered its long-promised profit inflection — about €36 million of adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) in 2025 — and holds a strong 20–25% share of a growing German streaming-TV market; its minority shareholders have opened a strategic-options process that could crystallize hidden value through a carve-out or sale. Three soft, non-binding levers could re-rate the shares if they break the company's way: a renegotiation of the punitive network-operator contract (management is in talks, targeting recovery of part of the roughly €50 million-a-year hit), completion of the JD.com cash-out of freenet's CECONOMY stake (offer price €4.60 per share, worth roughly €150 million), and the waipu.tv strategic review. The mobilezone acquisition adds real sales scale. For this to work, the earnings base must prove stable — not growing, just stable — and at least one of the three soft catalysts must land; a value investor is paid a high-single-digit dividend yield to wait.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a structurally disadvantaged, price-taking mobile reseller whose cheapness reflects a real and worsening problem, not a mispricing. freenet owns no network and no spectrum — it resells capacity from Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone, and Telefónica — so its mobile economics are ultimately set by the very counterparties it depends on. The network-operator contract signed in 2024 is direct proof of that vulnerability: it could strip up to €50 million of EBITDA a year from 2026 through 2028, and when a BNP Paribas analyst pressed management in February 2026 on what legal leverage freenet actually has, management refused to answer and even declined to confirm when the contract expires — the loudest possible tell on the biggest risk. Revenue has now fallen three years running (from €2.63 billion in 2023 to €2.44 billion in 2025), so the earnings-per-share growth is increasingly manufactured by share-count reduction and cost cuts, not demand. The 2024 'record' EBITDA leaned partly on a one-off sale of internet-protocol addresses. The balance sheet is no longer pristine: net debt rose to about €596 million after the debt-financed €340 million mobilezone deal, and the buyback was trimmed to roughly €60 million from the '€100 million' headline. waipu.tv subscriber targets were quietly re-based lower, and UBS models only about 200,000 net adds for 2026 versus management's 250,000–300,000 implied run-rate. Every forward catalyst is soft: the Telefónica renegotiation is unpredictable (UBS assumes only ~€25 million of the €50 million comes back), the CECONOMY cash-out is stuck in Austrian regulatory review with JD.com itself calling completion 'questionable,' and the waipu.tv review is third-party-driven with no timeline. Confirmation of the bear: the August 12 second-quarter print showing EBITDA down again, and a Telefónica outcome at or below €25 million recovery.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the right question is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power. Here the answer is: mostly no — the street has already re-priced this correctly. The stock fell about 29% this year as the ~€50 million-a-year network-operator hit, a weak 2026 EBITDA guide (€500–530M vs €547M consensus), and waipu.tv's slowdown all landed, and UBS closed out its bearish stance AFTER the plunge — a sign the easy short is over, not that a mispricing has opened. Where we do differ modestly from the most bearish view: consensus may be too pessimistic on the network-operator renegotiation (a partial ~€25M recovery is plausible) and is arguably assigning near-zero value to the waipu.tv strategic-options process and the CECONOMY cash-out. But those are options, not mispriced fundamentals. The street assumption we'd actually challenge is any bull who still cites the pre-dispute 'asset-light reseller deserves a premium' framing — the 2024 contract proved the carriers can claw margin back at will, so that premium thesis is broken.
forcing_function: There is no hard, dated catalyst that forces a re-rating. The three candidate events are all soft: (1) the Telefónica contract renegotiation — a non-binding, bilateral talk with an unpredictable outcome, targeted for the second half of 2026, that would require a stock-market announcement if guidance changes; (2) the CECONOMY / JD.com cash-out — an event freenet does not control, gated by Austrian regulators and flagged as 'questionable' by the acquirer; (3) the waipu.tv strategic-options process — third-party-initiated by Exaring's minority shareholders, with no announced timeline. The nearest dated event is simply the August 12 earnings date, which is a risk event, not a re-rating trigger. Absent a hard forcing function, this is a wait-and-collect-the-dividend situation, not a catalyst trade.
valley_of_death: The risky window over the next 3–9 months is concrete and adverse. First, the August 12 second-quarter print is expected to show group EBITDA down again (~−3% to ~€125M) — another confirmation of the contract drag before any relief. Second, the Telefónica renegotiation is expected to conclude in the second half of 2026 with an unpredictable outcome; anything at or below a ~€25M recovery (UBS's base case) disappoints, and a stalemate that pushes freenet toward the legal action management refused to discuss would be worse. Third, the CECONOMY cash-out — the cleanest source of ~€150M — is stuck in Austrian regulatory review, with JD.com itself warning completion 'is questionable'; a collapse or long delay removes a balance-sheet cushion the bulls are counting on. None of these is a cash-burn or maturity crisis (free cash flow is healthy, the bridge loan has a 12+6+6-month runway), but the news flow into year-end skews negative-to-neutral, not toward relief.
positioning_washout: Limited forced-selling dynamics. The shareholder base is yield-and-value-oriented, and the dividend was RAISED (to €2.07) rather than cut, so there is no mechanical income-fund exodus to trigger a capitulation low — the opposite of the classic dividend-cut washout. The ~29% decline already flushed the momentum and growth holders who were paying for the pre-dispute story. That means there is no obvious future forced-seller to create a better entry; the base here is relatively sticky, which caps both downside volatility and the odds of a violent, buyable flush.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. freenet is a real, cash-generative business at a cheap-looking ~7× free-cash-flow multiple with a ~9% dividend — but the deep-value signal is largely a fear-print on bad news that has already fired, not an un-played mispricing. Our sum-of-the-parts pins base fair value at roughly €22, which is slightly BELOW the €23.22 price; the adverse case is ~€18.5 (−20%) and the favorable case only ~€25 (+8%), so the risk/reward is symmetric-to-unfavorable even before we weigh the regime. Applying the current market regime sharpens the pass: this is a dispersion tape that rewards hard-dated, resolution-independent special-situations (forced-seller and spinoff windows are the fattest lane), and PENALIZES exactly what freenet offers — soft, serially-discussed, counterparty-dependent catalysts (a bilateral carrier renegotiation, a regulator-gated cross-border cash-out, a no-timeline carve-out review). The one load-bearing catalyst — the network-operator dispute — is a soft, non-binding negotiation whose bad leg already hit the tape; the good leg is uncertain and capped at partial recovery. The economic moat is narrow (an intangible-brand and distribution-scale edge, not a network) and eroding, with a material secular squeeze from a saturating German mobile market and structural dependence on the carriers freenet resells for. Net: a fairly-priced, slowly-eroding dividend payer, not an asymmetric special-situation. Verdict: pass for now, low conviction. Separately, the pure value case — cheap cash flow, covered dividend, a genuinely growing waipu.tv, honest but not fortress-like returns — is middling and fairly valued, not a bargain, and the eroding, narrow moat caps how much credit the optical cheapness earns.
sop_breakdown: Base-case reconciled fair value ≈ €22 per share, essentially at the current €23.22 price. Built from three operating parts plus one financial-asset overlay: (1) Mobile — the bulk of value at ~€2.0–2.3B enterprise value (roughly €380–400M EBITDA at ~5.5×), a low-growth reseller with the network-operator contract as the swing factor; (2) waipu.tv/IPTV — ~€330–360M (its ~€36M EBITDA at ~9–10×), the one growing, re-ratable part and the source of any strategic-review upside; (3) Media Broadcast — ~€550M (~€100M declining EBITDA at ~5.5×). Sum ≈ €2.9–3.0B enterprise value, less ~€596M net debt ≈ €2.3–2.4B equity, plus the CECONOMY stake at ~€120M (carrying value ~€142M haircut for JD.com deal-completion risk) ≈ €2.5B, or roughly €21–22 per share. The screener's ~14% margin of safety is largely spent after the ~29% share-price fall.
risk_reward: Roughly symmetric, mildly unfavorable. Downside-to-break: base fair value ~€22 sits ~5% BELOW the €23.22 price, and the adverse case is ~€18.5 (about −20%). Upside-to-fair-value: the favorable case is ~€25 (about +8%), with a free-cash-flow-capitalization stretch to ~€28. So the setup is ~−20% downside vs ~+8–20% upside, cushioned by a ~9% dividend yield that pays you to wait. Not the asymmetric payoff a special-situation demands.
catalyst_status_plain: a soft catalyst, no fixed date
peer_comps_note: Peers are the German network-owning carriers (Deutsche Telekom, Telefónica, Vodafone) and European MVNOs; the house comp read flags freenet as cheap-versus-peers at ~7× price/free-cash-flow. We DISCOUNT that lever: the gap to facilities-based carriers is not idiosyncratic single-name alpha — it is a legitimate structural discount for a business that owns no network and, as the 2024 network-operator contract just demonstrated, has its margin set by the carriers it resells for. The comp read argues freenet's asset-light model 'deserves a premium, not a discount'; the contract dispute is live evidence to the contrary. We therefore anchor to the sum-of-the-parts (~€22), not to a peer-premium multiple, and treat the peer cheapness as partly earned, not free.

- **2026-02 (FY25, new CEO Robin Harries):** the story flips. The same long-term contract praised a year earlier is now called a "sick agreement": up to EUR 13M EBITDA hit in 2025 and up to EUR 50M a year for 2026-28 because volume commitments with one network operator (reported as Telefonica Deutschland) were not met. The narrative pivots to value-over-volume pricing, the mobilezone Germany acquisition (+240k subscribers), an "AI-first" operating model, and the freenet premium brand.

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record year" 2024 (2025-03) | FY24 net income EUR 247M vs 155M in 2023, but helped by a one-off IP-address sale; revenue fell from EUR 2.63B to 2.48B | Partly flattered by a one-off |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
**Stable-to-declining in substance, rising in rhetoric.** Vilanek (2025) was specific and confident. Harries (2026) is upbeat ("very pleased", "exciting") but more evasive on the one issue that matters: on the network contract the CFO said "I do not want to talk about it" (2026-02) and "Do I have an agreement today? No" (2026-08). The CFO also called reaching the 2026 EBITDA guidance "challenging" (2026-08) - a defensive tell that rests on second-half commissions, lower marketing and seasonal advertising.

Subscriber targets were met or beaten (306k organic postpaid net adds in 2025). - **The network contract** (BNP's Joshua Mills, 2026-02): what legal leverage does a reseller have, and does the contract roll beyond 2028? Answer: no detail; "I have not said that it ends in '28". This is the recurring non-answer.
- **ARPU and back book** (Kepler, 2026-08): when does the average revenue per user stop falling? Answer: H2-27.
- **waipu market share** (Deutsche Bank, 2026-08): waipu only held share in a growing market while Magenta (Deutsche Telekom) pushed hard.
- **Tax rate** (2026-08): H1 effective tax looked like 33%; CFO insists ~19%.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: the "sick agreement" (2026-02) - a contract signed in 2024 that management sold as stability is now the main earnings drag; resolution is in a third party's hands with no date.
- Red: underlying EBITDA and FCF declining in H1-26 while the headline revenue rises on an acquisition.
- Red: no clarity on network-contract terms beyond 2028 - for a reseller, the contracts are the business.
- Red: guidance called "challenging" by the CFO (2026-08).

- The new CEO blaming "the former management" for brand-marketing contracts and the network deal - a kitchen-sink posture that lowers the bar but also means the old contract framing was not trustworthy.
- "AI-first" language (voicebot Finn, AI Buddy) replaces the old Vilanek metrics (EBITDA per employee); cost-cutting levers are being positioned as the swing factor.
- Partnership with 1&1 (scaling since 2026-02) diversifies network partners - quiet hedge against the operator with which freenet is in dispute.
- The stock has fallen from EUR 36.94 to EUR 21.74 over the last year; peer file still describes it as "at its 52-week high", which is now stale.

**Trajectory: STABLE** - the cash engine and dividend are intact, the earnings base is shrinking modestly and has not yet bottomed. **Moat:** narrow - scale in German retail distribution (shops, MediaMarktSaturn, mobilezone channels) and a strong IPTV product, but no network ownership and a gross margin of ~26% that is set by others. ROIC ~10.7% is decent and roughly stable; the gross margin is stable. **Secular threat:** manageable - the linear-TV part (freenet TV, ~500k subscribers and falling) is in secular decline but small; waipu.tv is on the winning side of cord-cutting; the real risk is contractual, not structural. The cheapness is mostly a fair print of a shrinking-then-stabilising earnings base with a contract overhang, not a fear-print on a growing franchise.
